metadata.file_name: 168. Chen et al. (2021). Discrimination of the Contextual Features of Top Performers in Scientific Literacy Using a Machine Learning Approach.pdf
metadata.title: Discrimination of the Contextual Features of Top Performers in Scientific Literacy Using a Machine Learning Approach

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2015 science scores and questionnaire responses for 15-year-old students, restricted to countries/economies that administered the computer-based science assessment components. The analytic sample is further restricted to students with available student and principal questionnaire responses, and the authors report cleaning to remove a large proportion of missing values. For the binary target (top performers vs non-top performers), the authors explicitly state that PISA student sampling weights were fully considered to obtain unbiased population estimates. The manuscript does not report replicate-weight methods (e.g., BRR/jackknife), and the ML pipeline (SVM with SVM-RFE and 10-fold cross-validation) is implemented in Python/scikit-learn; thus, the paper’s handling of complex-survey variance estimation for ML metrics is not fully specified beyond the use of PISA weights.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used PISA 2015 science domain data for 15-year-old students from 58 countries/economies that administered the computer-based assessment mode for the science components. The target is defined using PV1SCIE (first plausible value for science) with a proficiency cutoff at PV > 633.33 to classify top performers (levels 5–6) vs non-top performers (below level 5). Only student and principal questionnaires were required across countries; optional parent/teacher questionnaires were not used. The authors report cleaning and then imputing missing values (school-level imputation using student responses within the same school; remaining school-level missing imputed via nearest-neighbor mean; remaining student-level missing imputed via nearest-neighbor), followed by normalization.

main_findings.target_variable: Top performer in science literacy (PV1SCIE levels 5–6 vs below level 5)
main_findings.performance_metrics: SVM with SVM-RFE feature selection; optimal top-20 feature set. Candidate sets: Top-10 accuracy 64.02% ± 4.34%, Top-20 accuracy 69.52% ± 4.40%, Top-30 accuracy 69.06% ± 3.72%. Two follow-up 10-fold CV rounds (top-20): Round 1 accuracy 77.50%, recall 78.48%; Round 2 accuracy 75.80%, recall 76.39%.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 Science the study leveraged perceived feedback, parental education/occupational status, disciplinary climate, learning time/involvement, school ICT resources, teacher quantity, and science self-efficacy to classify top performers (PV1SCIE levels 5–6) versus non-top performers, finding that teacher instructional practices, family socioeconomic status, classroom disciplinary climate, learning time/involvement, school media/ICT resources, teacher quantity, and student self-efficacy were the most predictive contextual features. This indicates that science excellence policies should prioritize classroom-level instructional feedback/adaptation and supportive learning environments alongside family-support and early learning investments, while recognizing that the results are predictive (not causal) and rely on questionnaire-based contextual measures.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzes PISA 2015 science literacy for 380,771 secondary students from 58 countries/economies, restricting to those using the computer-based science assessment components and using only student and principal questionnaires. The dependent variable is a binary indicator of “top performers” defined by PV1SCIE (first plausible value for science) with a cutoff at PV > 633.33 (levels 5–6). The authors apply SVM with SVM-RFE to rank 141 contextual variables and select an optimal top-20 feature set, then evaluate classification via 10-fold cross-validation. The top-20 set achieves about 69.52% accuracy in the initial selection stage and 77.50% (recall 78.48%) and 75.80% (recall 76.39%) in two follow-up 10-fold CV rounds. Limitations include reliance on self-reported questionnaire/contextual variables, imputation/normalization steps, and the fact that predictive feature importance does not establish causal effects.
